title.narrative: Capacity Development Support for Auditor General's Office, Maldives

description.narrative: " Development Objective The project development objective of the proposed project is to enhance the scope and impact of audit services provided by the Auditor General's Office of the Republic of Maldives. Description of the IDF - Financed Components, Activities and Outcomes The project consists of the following 4 components which are described in detail below: 1.0 Audit Planning and HR Management 2.0 Financial Statement Audits 3.0 Performance Audits 4.0 Audit Impact The project development objective of the proposed project is ""to enhance the scope and quality of audit services provided by the Auditor General's Office of the Republic of Maldives."" The anticipated effectiveness date of the project is July/August, 2012, and estimated completion date is August, 2015. The major activities and outputs of the components of the proposed project are outlined below. 1. Component: Audit Planning and HR Management (US$) The Auditor General's Office has a mandate to audit the accounts of some 37 line ministries and departments comprising 198 spending units. In addition, the Auditor General is responsible for the audits of 69 State-Owned Enterprises, and he may be entrusted to audit the project financial statements of foreign-aided projects. Further, there are ongoing discussions that may result in requiring the Auditor General's Office to audit the accounts of some 220 recently established local councils. This component of the project will enable the Auditor General to better manage scarce resources to effectively discharge his mandate through the following activities. Outcome: Audit resources are effectively managed to economically and efficiently discharge the audit mandate o 1.1 Activity: Refine the audit plans of the Auditor General's Office Currently, the annual work plans of the Office represent theoretical ideal standards rather than realistic estimates that can be used to manage and control the work of the Office. Rough formulas based on aggregate expenditures and revenues are applied taking into consideration statutory reporting deadlines in order to develop the plans, but there is inadequate reflection of relative risks or complexities of audits, and the work plans are not adjusted in the event of budget revisions. It is not practicable to examine every public entity's accounts annually. The Auditor General' Office, has secured external assistance (using its own resources) to develop an audit plan, which will be realistic, ensure that appropriate audit coverage is provided dependent upon the risks involved and utilizing outsourced audit services where appropriate. The Plan will facilitate monitoring of progress by senior management which should help improve delivery and reduce slippages. The main thrust of the initial plan will be to help the Office achieve its statutory deadline of 31 May 2013 for the completion of its 2012 central Government audits. The audit plans will be tied to staffing and budget requests, and sent to the Public Accounts Committee. 1.1.1. Output: Annual work plans notified to PAC and used to monitor work flows 1.2 Activity: Devise and implement an audit management system A cost-effective means of monitoring the timely completion of audits and of ensuring the quality of work done needs to be devised and implemented. This activity will include (a) tools such as a time recording and audit milestone reporting system; (b) new procedures such as for supervision and review, quality control, and reliance on the work of another auditor. The activity will include support in monitoring the work of the Office during the period of the project, and providing advice in identifying and removing bottlenecks and improving work flows. This activity will be undertaken using the Office's own resources. 1.2.1 Output: Time recording and audit milestone reporting system 1.2.2 Output: Quality control procedures 1.3 Activity: Refine HR policies to align with corporate objectives The sustained improvement in financial audit and the ability of the Auditor General's Office to improve the timeliness of its deliveries will only be achieved with better staff management practices. This activity will therefore include a comprehensive review of HR policies primarily in relation to work flow issues identified above. To help improve the effectiveness of audit staff, practical help and support will be provided to: - Improve individual responsibility and delivery through better objective setting and monitoring - Ensure effective delegation - Improve time management - Help staff better manage their auditees In terms of wider HR systems practical help will be provided to introduce staff performance appraisal procedures, the use of competencies to complement academic qualifications for both recruitment and promotions, better management of sick absences and procedures for identifying training needs across the Office. The Auditor General's Office currently uses the TeamMate audit software package for documenting its audit work. This component of the project will also assess how the Office would benefit from the other TeamMate modules, for example, to aid work scheduling and resource planning and in using the TeamRisk module. 1.3.1 Output: Revised HR policies aligned to corporate deliveries 2.0 Component 2 Financial Statement Audits This is a priority for the Auditor General's Office. The Public Finance Act and regulations require all ""accountable offices"" to prepare financial statements in accordance with International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) beginning with the December 31, 2009 year-end. Because government has only begun to produce financial statements, audit to date has been limited to compliance tests of transactions. The audit manual developed in 1999 and the financial audit guides produced in 2007 were never tested on audits of financial statements, and there is a need to upgrade the audit reference materials to meet the current International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI) framework for financial statement audits. Outcome: o Financial statement audits are conducted by the Auditor General's Office in compliance with Levels 1-4 of the ISSAI framework for financial audits 2.1 Activity: Upgrade the Financial Audit Manual This activity will document the audit standards and procedures to be followed by the Auditor General's Office in conducting and reporting on the results of its financial statement audits. As already stated the Auditor General's Office has recently embarked on a project to improve the standard of its financial audits. In particular to ensure that they comply with International Auditing Standards. The work will also ensure that a risk-based approach is adopted t. This activity will also ensure that this is supported by a Financial Audit Manual which will include detailed audit programs, guidelines and templates that can be used for the audits of the financial statements of various kinds of public sector entities. While the bulk of this activity will be undertaken using the Auditors General's Office's own resource, at the end of the 2012 audit cycle, the IDF project would review the audit guidance material to ensure that it reflects the current ISSAI framework for financial statement audits particularly including ISSAI 1240 on the auditor's responsibilities relating to fraud in an audit of financial statements. 2.1.1 Output: Financial Audit Manual and audit guides 2.2 Activity: Conduct financial statement audits Using the Auditor General's Office's own resources, the project will ensure that audits for the 2012 financial year are planned and undertaken in line with International Auditing Standards, and to make best use of limited resource, a risk-based approach will be introduced for each audit. Staff will be trained in financial audit concepts, such as confidence levels, materiality and risk and be able to use these in a practical way to develop robust audit plans. Teams will also be coached through the fieldwork and reporting stages. 2.2.1 Output: Financial statement audit reports tabled in Parliament 2.3 Activity: Provide specialist training in financial statement audits While the Auditor General's Office's own initiative will address the overall financial audit, the IDF project will provide more specific assistance in key areas. For example the audit of Revenue has been somewhat patchy in the past and the Auditor General's Office has no experience at all of auditing the consolidation of the State accounts or the statements on public debt. The project will include courses on: - donor PFS requirements for project audits, - building up an IT audit capability in the Office including both practical audits and classroom- based training; - practical assistance in developing an approach to the audit of the State's Consolidated Accounts; - training and practical application in the use of CAATs, particularly in the selection of transactions (note: project costing to include additional licences if required); and - Assistance in developing approaches to the audit of Revenue and Public Debt. In all areas auditors will be selected and trained as future trainers. This activity will include technical training courses in aspects of financial auditing, complete with the learning objectives, presentations, case studies and instructor notes for each course. 2.3.1 Output: Auditors trained in specialist aspects of financial statement audits Component 3: Performance Audits The Audit Act provides the Auditor General with a discretionary mandate to conduct performance audits, but no such audits have been conducted due to a lack of professional skills and performance audit methodologies. At the same time, there have been increasing demands for performance audits from the Public Accounts Committee, in line with demands from PACs in other countries of the region and globally. o Performance audit capabilities are introduced to the Auditor General's Office 3.1 Activity: Prepare a performance audit manual The performance audit manuals of the SAIs of India, Bhutan and other countries will be reviewed for their relevance to the Maldives, and used as a basis for drafting a performance audit manual that incorporates the current ISSAI framework for performance audits. The manual will be field tested on the pilot audits conducted in activity 3.2 and revised based on pilot audit experiences. 3.1.1. Output: Performance audit manual approved by the Auditor General 3.2 Activity: Conduct pilot performance audits Three pilot performance audits will be selected, including government privatizations and perhaps one procurement audit and one environmental audit. The possibility of including other stakeholders such as Tender Evaluation Board or the Ministry of Environment, Energy and Water on the teams formed for performance audits of procurement or environment, respectively, will be explored. The pilot performance audit teams will be provided with classroom training on the draft Performance Audit Manual immediately prior to the audits and with on-the-job training during all aspects of the pilot performance audits. 3.2.1. Output: Performance audit reports tabled in Parliament 3.3 Activity: Provide training in performance audits Classroom training materials for performance audit will be developed based on the performance audit manual produced in activity 3.1 and using case study materials developed from the pilot audits conducted in activity 3.2. Selected persons from the pilot performance audit teams will be supplied with training of trainers and supported during delivery of the first round of training. All training materials will be revised and, where appropriate, new training materials will be developed and additional training of trainers delivered based on the results of the classroom training. 3.3.1. Output: Performance audit training courses, materials and trainers Component 4: Audit Impact Components 2 and 3 of the proposed project will enable the Auditor General's Office to shift the focus of its audit services from transactions-oriented compliance audits to risk-based financial audits and to performance audits. Stakeholders in Maldives, however, will not necessarily understand why such a shift is important or what role is played by the Auditor General's Office in general. For example, there is currently some confusion as to the Auditor General's role in respect of internal audit, prescribing accounting standards, setting financial reporting formats, and detecting instances of fraud and corruption. This component of the project will enable AGO to measure and report to its stakeholders on the value and benefits of external audit. Outcome: Stakeholders in Maldives understand the value and benefits of the Auditor General's Office 4.1 Activity: Design and implement a communications/PR strategy This activity will include consultations with major stakeholders, analysis of their positions, and design of proactive actions that could be taken to enhance relations with each major stakeholder group. Major stakeholders include the Public Accounts Committee, other accountability institutions such as the Anti-Corruption Commission and the Police, the Executive, the media, and NGO's and the general public. For the PAC, possible actions that could be pursued under this activity might include orientation sessions for new members, training on public accounts and the role of the Auditor General, informal meetings with the Chair to brief on audit reports immediately before tabling, or planning meetings to establish the priorities for committee hearings. For the Executive, possible actions could include reviewing summaries of recent audit recommendations or conducting seminars on the role of internal and external audit. For the media, the routine use of media releases and media conferences could be developed. And for the general public, the use of brochures, videos, website and social media could be explored. 4.1.1. Output: Communications/PR strategy approved by the Auditor General 4.2 Activity: Propose possible legislative amendments to better align audit responsibilities This activity will include a review of the existing Audit Act, Public Finance Act, and Constitution to identify apparent deficiencies, discrepancies and anomalies. It will also include several rounds of stakeholder workshops to build consensus around the possible solutions, which may involve inviting senior finance or audit officers from other countries to the Maldives to participate in the stakeholder workshops. 4.2.1. Output: draft Audit Bill approved by the Auditor General and endorsed by the Public Accounts Committee and the Ministry of Finance. 4.3 Activity: Conduct performance assessment A performance measurement assessment tool for SAIs is currently under development by INTOSAI and is expected to be disseminated during the term of the project. This activity supports a self-assessment application of the SAI Performance Measurement Framework that is currently under development. The assessment will be used in conjunction with activity 4.1 detailed activities, and to inform future refinements of the strategic development plan of the Auditor General's Office. 4.3.1. Output: self-assessment of the performance of the Auditor General's Office using the SAI PMF endorsed by INTOSAI published on AGO website Key Monitoring Indicators (maximum of three) Progress made under any resulting grant will be monitored according to these indicators: Indicator 1: Number of financial statement audits conducted in accordance with ISSAI framework and reported to Parliament Base Value:Nil Date:July 2012 Target:9 Date:June 2015 Indicator 2: Number of performance audits conducted in accordance with ISSAI framework and reported to Parliament Base Value:Nil Date: July 2012 Target: 3 Date: July 2015 Indicator 3: Current year audit observations implemented by the executive within 1 year Base Value:<35% Date:July 2012 Target: 50% Date:July 2015"
